div.head: Chapter 4
div.p: The fourth kind or category of unbelievers is those who neither hold usurped lands that were once ours, nor have wrongfully despoiled us of them. Likewise, those who have never done us any injury, harm, or wrong, nor have any intention of doing so; who neither harm nor impede our holy faith, whether because they have never heard it, or because for good or ill they have no concern for it whatsoever. Likewise, those who neither in the present nor in past ages were subjects of the Christian Empire or of any member of the Church, in law or in fact, that is, in act, whether by reason of origin or of domicile, or by reason of any offense committed against us or against the Church, or by reason of contract, or by any other cause of subjection of the kinds we listed above; as there are many nations in the world that are free of all such charges. This applies especially if there were found any pagans or gentiles who have their own kingdoms, regions, provinces, and native lands apart from ours, which they occupied before any other peoples and which belonged to no others. And so too all other nations, peoples, and peoples: Greeks, barbarians, Tartars, Persians, Macedonians, Scythians, Massagetae, Syracusans, Troglodytes, Dacians, Nomads, Sogdians, Bactrians, Albanians, Cumans, Indians or people of India, Ethiopians, Turks, Saracens; those who worship idols, those who honor or believe in Muhammad, or those who are filled with abominable superstitions and errors and abominable vices: provided that in the ways mentioned above, or by any of them, they do not offend the Catholic faith or the Christian commonwealth. All of these, I say, the aforementioned, and if there are yet others of this kind, we place them in this fourth category; and consequently, with them or with any of them we have nothing to do: "for what have we to do with judging those who are outside?" 1 Corinthians 5, beyond loving them as ourselves, and endeavoring through teaching and good example to bring them and win them to Christ: De penitentia, dist. 2, c. charitas, el 29. These have their regions, their provinces, their kingdoms, their dominions, their kings, their high and low jurisdictions, their judges and magistrates and their territories, within which they exercise their power legitimately and may freely use it; and within those territories no king in the world, without violating natural law, is permitted to enter without the leave of their kings or their commonwealths, still less to exercise or practice any jurisdiction or power whatsoever. All of this stands proved by the first principle and by all the canonists in the chapter que in ecclesiarum, De constitutionibus, and by Innocent in cap. quod super his, De voto; and more plainly than other jurists, Baldo in L. decernimus, Codex, De sacrosancta Ecclesia, where he says this: "Provinces that are not accustomed to being ruled by princes must remain under the natural dominion of their own rulers, that is, by right of nations." ff. De iustitia et iure, L. ex hoc iure. And if another seizes dominion there against the will of the king or prince, that person is a tyrant, and therefore the usurped dominions are called tyrannies.

Well suited to this purpose is what Bartolus says in the book hostes, ff, De captivis et postliminio, that there are some peoples with whom we have no peace, no war, and no other dealings, and he gives the example of those who dwell in India, and concludes thus: "that we have nothing to do with those who are outside," that is to say: those who live outside our borders and territories, provided they do not offend us in any of the said ways; and still less with those whom we never knew even existed in the world.
